passages.text: The question: What does Madhyasth Darshan mean by spirituality and realisation, what practice leads to realisation, and how would anyone know it had occurred? How does its answer compare with Advaita Vedanta’s path of knowledge, and with what modern philosophy and contemplative science have established about practice and religious experience?

This study examines anubhav — realisation — and the practice Madhyasth Darshan holds leads to it. The darshan presents its account of these matters as anubhavatmak adhyatmvad, realisation-centred spiritualism (AVD, p. 2), and the account is compared here with Advaita Vedanta, whose path of knowledge is its nearest and most demanding rival, and with modern Western philosophy and contemplative science, which turn out to have a great deal to say about this subject and not what one might expect.

The relevance of modern philosophy is worth stating in advance, because the natural assumption is that spiritual practice lies outside its range. It does not. Ancient philosophy was itself organised around spiritual exercises, as Hadot’s work established; the epistemology of religious experience is a developed field; the perennialist–constructivist dispute is exactly the question of whether contemplative states have content independent of the tradition that trains them; L. A. Paul’s account of transformative experience formalises the problem of appraising a state one has not undergone; and contemplative science has produced both suggestive findings and a serious methodological reckoning. Each bears directly on claims the darshan makes.

The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.6 states the transmission and evidence conditions in outline and §§7.1–7.5 records the resulting evidential problems; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.14 sets out realisation in coexistence as an activity of jeevan; and The Sixty-One Activity Pairs of Jeevan records the 122 activities of jeevan pair by pair. This study takes the practice itself as its subject: what is done, which activities of jeevan it makes effective and how, what is claimed to result, and what would count as knowing that it had.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that realisation is the understanding of existence as coexistence — of every unit saturated in one omnipresent reality — reached by jeevan through study and the refinement of its own activities, and evidenced in behaviour, work, and the capacity to convey it. It denies that any absorbed state is itself a knowing, and it says so on the strength of its founder’s report that he attained such a state and found no knowing in it. That denial separates the darshan most sharply from the traditions it emerged from. What replaces the absorbed state is a positive account: spirituality as the understanding of the omnipresent, realisation as the awakening of all ten activities of jeevan and their evidence in 122 named conducts, and liberation as release from delusion.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 Spirituality as the understanding of the omnipresent

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The darshan uses the word adhyatma, spirit, for the omnipresent reality itself. Every unit in existence — atom, plant, animal, human — is saturated in one all-pervading, non-active reality, and the darshan’s name for its account of spirituality comes from that fact:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “One of the names I have given to this omnipresent reality is ‘adhyatma’ (spirit). This scripture has been named as ‘Realisation Centred Spiritualism’ because all the units are seen to be submerged, soaked & surrounded in this omnipresent reality.” — AVD, p. 236

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The same reality is called Omnipotence (satta), Brahma, space, and knowledge. Knowledge itself is the omnipresent Omnipotence, referred to as space, and it is called paramatma for being subtler than atma (MVD, p. 35); omnipresence is what the word God refers to (MVD, p. 163). Humans have the opportunity to understand, study, and experiment with three aspects of existence — the spiritual, which is the omnipresent; the deific, which is the intellectual or sentient; and the metaphysical, which is insentient nature — and every man and woman has the right to realisation and experimentation in coexistence (MVD, p. 285). The spiritual accomplishment is named precisely: atma-bodh, the enlightenment of the self, is itself the spiritual accomplishment (MVD, p. 286), and upon definitive understanding, as buddhi turns towards atma, atma-bodh and Brahma-realisation — realisation in coexistence — come into effect together (MVD, pp. 286–287).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Two consequences follow for practice. Spirituality is not a domain of experience set apart from ordinary life: the omnipresent is present in everything, so understanding it is understanding the whole of existence and oneself within it. And spiritual knowledge is not ineffable. The idealist scriptures and mystery-based contemplation hold knowledge to be unmanifest and ineffable; this darshan holds that knowledge is manifest, effable, and understandable through study, and that its evidence becomes accessible to all through behaviour (MVD, p. 4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The founder’s own questions set the terms of the account. How could the world be false if it arose from Brahma, the truth? How could Brahma be the cause of both bondage and liberation? And what counts as evidence — the word or its bearer, the credible saying or its originator, the scripture or its author (MVD, pp. 4–6)? The darshan’s answers to these three questions organise what follows: Brahma is truth and the world is perpetual (MVD, p. 13); bondage is delusion and liberation is its removal (§1.5); and the awakened human alone is the basis of evidence (SB, p. 5).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 What realisation is

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realisation has a definite object and a definite location. It is realisation in the ultimate truth which is in the form of coexistence, distinguished from contemplation, the awareness of truth (MVD, p. 316). Its object is not something absent that practice must bring into being. Omnipotence in the form of omnipresence has been uniformly inherent in every entity since eternity, and its realisation is the goal of humans (MVD, p. 317); truth is present even before awakening (MVD, p. 303); and while union with any finite thing is attained and lost, no entity or activity is ever without the pre-existing union with the omnipresent, which can only be realised (MVD, p. 302). What study and practice develop is the capacity, ability, and receptivity for that realisation, which is the right of every human being (MVD, p. 302). Realisation is an activity of atma (MVD, pp. 204, 307), and its effect is transmitted to buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun (MVD, p. 318).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Its content is given as three kinds of knowledge — of existence as coexistence, of jeevan, and of humane conduct (MVD, pp. 13, 127, 300; KD, p. 30). Complete enlightenment is the enlightenment of these three, and it is called enlightenment of the self (MVD, p. 300): an awakened human has the awareness of their own being and of the being of the entire existence (MVD, p. 84). Awakening is correspondingly defined as knowing, believing, recognising, and fulfilling jeevan and existence as they are (AVD, p. 259). Realisation is thus neither a feeling nor a vision. It is the understanding, obtained through the natural progression of things, of their states and motions, their emergence and their results (MVD, p. 77).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Each kind of knowledge has determinate content. To understand any existing thing is to understand its rup, gun, swabhav, and dharma — form, property, essential nature, and innateness (MVD, p. 273). Rup is determined by shape, volume, and density; gun is the generative, degenerative, and mediative; swabhav differs across the four orders; and dharma is cumulative across them — existence in the material order, growth along with existence in the biological, the hope of living along with both in the animal, and happiness along with all three in the knowledge order (MVD, pp. 50–51). Form, property, and essential nature can be understood; dharma can only be realised (MVD, p. 273). Visualisation of all four, together with generative, degenerative, and mediative knowledge, is the innateness of chitta, where sakshatkar, direct recognition, takes place (MVD, pp. 126, 203–204).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge of humane conduct is specified by justice, dharma, and truth. Deciding justice and injustice, dharma and adharma, truth and untruth is the innateness of vritti (MVD, pp. 203–204), and the three are levels of realisation itself: justice is the manifestation of realisation in behaviour, dharma the manifestation of realisation in thought, and coexistence the realisation in atma that is the ultimate truth (MVD, p. 156). Correct evaluation occurs only through awakening; otherwise over-, under-, or mis-evaluation takes place (MVD, p. 203). Knowledge reaches conduct through law, regulation, and balance:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Knowledge itself is law; law itself is regulation; regulation itself is balance; balanced living itself is justice in humans; living within the universal orderliness with justice itself is dharma, i.e., resolution; realisation in coexistence itself is dharma and truth.” — MVD, p. 174

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The six of niyam, niyantran, santulan, nyaya, dharma, and satya — law, regulation, balance, justice, dharma, and truth — are evidenced in the fruition of realisation (MVD, p. 80). It follows that a person cannot have realised and still misjudge, or have realised and still live unregulated, and the darshan states the observable mark: absence of mistakes and crimes in behaviour characterises complete awakening, and it is observed in human interactions (MVD, p. 285). This is what makes the account testable in principle; §6.3 examines how much the test establishes.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: What is realised is not private. The study is in, by, and for realisation in coexistence (MVD, p. 35), and what is realised can be stated, taught, and lived. Whatever cannot be conveyed has not, on this account, been realised.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Anubhav is one stage of four — sakshatkar, bodh, anubhav, praman — whose relations §1.11 sets out. Where this study says “realisation” without qualification it means anubhav; where the distinction between the stages matters, the Hindi terms are used.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 Samadhi without knowing

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The account of practice begins with a negative finding reported in the first person. Shri A. Nagraj records that he was assured by the scholars and sages of his time that the only way to know the unknown is samadhi, accepted this, went to Amarkantak, and practised from 1950 with maturity in the 1960s (MVD, p. 7). The practice was traditional. He followed the Agama-Tantra method of upasana, which seeks samadhi by visualising the deities in every part of the body (nyas), until one day he found himself free of their imagined proximity: the awareness of “I am” remained, there were no other thoughts, and there was no thought of achieving, having, or doing anything (JV, p. 12). His practice also followed the instructions available for nididhyasan, samadhi, control of the mind, and the method of observing (AVD, p. 72). The result is stated without hedging:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “In 1970, I accepted that I had attained samadhi. In this state, my hopes, thoughts, and desires were silent, and it was clear that the event of ‘knowing the unknown’ did not occur.” — MVD, p. 7

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The state recurred for twelve to eighteen hours a day (MVD, p. 7). It answered none of his questions: he received no answers from understanding Vedanta and none after achieving samadhi (JV, p. 13), and the thoughtless state, whether called samadhi, nididhyasan, complete enlightenment, or nirvana, did not supply them (AVD, p. 72). Nor could the state serve as evidence of itself:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “There was nothing to describe in the state of samadhi; how could I present its evidence?” — JV, p. 13

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Two distinct claims are being made, and they should not be run together. The first is phenomenological: in samadhi hope, thought, and desire fall silent — mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi have no remaining motion (AVD, p. 220) — and no knowing occurs. The state is not nothing. It yields what the traditions call self-limited happiness (svantah sukh), free of fear, temptation, and the pain of lack (AVD, p. 220), and Nagraj counts himself among the very few who have reached it (AVD, p. 222). The second claim is evidential: because there is nothing in the state to describe, it cannot serve as evidence of anything, including of itself. The second is the more consequential, and it is a demand for public checkability made from inside a contemplative tradition rather than against it.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The darshan draws a practical conclusion as well. No programme of living arises in the thoughtless state, so the person’s usefulness becomes zero (AVD, p. 220); during the pursuit of samadhi the seeker cannot take part in family, society, or the system of living (AVD, p. 165); and the method of silence is completely against the natural manifestation of jeevan, whose activity never ceases (AVD, p. 74).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 Samyama, and an inverted ladder

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: What Nagraj reports as productive is samyama, and he undertook it to test the samadhi he could not otherwise evidence (JV, p. 13). Patanjali’s definition — dharana, dhyana, and samadhi practised on one object — is cited and then departed from:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “I could not agree with what was written about samyama. Hence, I devised my own design and method of samyama and subsequently carried it out.” — JV, p. 13

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The design he adopted inverts the received order:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Of my own accord, I accepted the sequence of samadhi, dhyan, and dharana as the process for samyama. Two years later, having accomplished samyama, I accepted the evidence of having attained samadhi.” — MVD, p. 7

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Its object is stated separately. In the thoughtless state, together with the acceptance of existence, all realities were seen to be ceaselessly immersed in space, and this prompted samyama on space itself; soon after, existence presented itself in its true form, as coexistence, and jeevan was seen within it (AVD, p. 72). Seeing, here, means understanding (JV, p. 13; AVD, p. 87). The reported outcome is realisation that all existence is in the form of coexistence, presented in literary form for study (MVD, p. 7) — a state in which the understanding can be imparted, together with sight of the jeevan atom and of the three stages of wanting to live, to be happy, and to evidence oneself (JV, pp. 13–14).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Patanjali’s sequence ascends from holding to absorption. This one runs from absorption back through attention to dharana, a word the darshan elsewhere defines as innateness, that which cannot be separated from a thing (MVD, p. 43). The darshan presents samyama not as traditional authority but as a method its author devised because the received one did not satisfy him, and it does not recommend the route to others (§1.12). §6.1 takes up what the texts do and do not explain about the sequence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 Mystery, delusion, and liberation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The darshan names its target rahasya, mystery, and defines it as a deficiency of understanding rather than a property of reality:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Not revealing understanding or not being able to do so, or not being able to attain it, is a mystery. The incapacity for this is ‘mysteriousness’.” — MVD, p. 273

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Mystery is also the incompleteness in understanding the absolute state and activity, and its eradication comes only through the holistic view of reality, which yields certitude (MVD, p. 209). Beneath mystery lies delusion, belief different from reality (MVD, p. 291), whose root is the assumption that the body is jeevan (MVD, pp. 80–81; AVD, p. 88). Delusion is at the root of all unhappiness (MVD, p. 318), and it shows as excess, deficiency, and omission in visualisation and as over-, under-, and mis-evaluation in judgement (MVD, p. 286; AVD, p. 55).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The hope for liberation is found in all humans. The darshan distinguishes liberation from unhappiness and liberation from delusion, notes that all study, worship, experimentation, behaviour, vocation, practice, and dedication have been undertaken for these, and presents its own proposal as one for liberation from delusion (MVD, p. 149). It gives the old question of bondage and liberation a definite answer. What is bound, what binds, and what is freed is jeevan itself (AVD, pp. 139, 150). Bondage takes three forms: bondage of hope, directed at sensory gratification; bondage of thought, which takes one’s own thoughts to be superior; and bondage of desire, which takes the maximisation of physical creation to be superior (AVD, pp. 155, 167). To be free from the bondage of delusion is moksha, and this is the evidence of awakening (AVD, p. 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The liberated condition is described in the traditions’ own vocabulary. The complete acceptance and realisation of the mortality of the body, the immortality and continuity of jeevan, and the laws of work and behaviour is seedless (nirbeej) thought; behaviour in accordance with it is seedless behaviour; and this is liberation from delusion (MVD, p. 81). The jeevan-mukta — one liberated while living, who has moved irreversibly out of animal consciousness and delusion — does not suffer from the recollection of the past or apprehension of the future and has no resistance with the present (MVD, p. 81), and nurturing and advancing human society is their essential nature (MVD, p. 157). The state of realisation is named kaivalya, absoluteness, in which there is liberation from suffering, resentment, fear, and the bondage of delusion (MVD, pp. 317–318). Kaivalya is evidenced as participation in the whole of orderliness together with expression, communication, and exposition; the positive form of liberation from bondage is awakening completeness, and kaivalya lies in awakening, not in moksha (AVD, pp. 260–261). For one who is evidence in that state, no further bodily journeys are needed (AVD, p. 261).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The goal of practice is therefore neither an encounter nor a dissolution of the self. It is the removal of a cognitive deficit, delusion, from which the ending of suffering follows. A deluded jeevan keeps yearning for a happiness the five senses cannot supply (MVD, p. 274), and the accomplishment of mental wellbeing or bliss is itself liberation from mystery (MVD, p. 301).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6 Study as practice

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The positive method is study, and the darshan states it in the vocabulary of worship:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Study itself is worship. The authentic human is the teacher, in whose proximity study takes place.” — MVD, p. 150

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Through study one attains the authority of innateness and independence by coming into absolute-resonance and absolute-accordance with understanding (MVD, p. 150). Study is defined by what it discriminates: understanding the difference between the laws necessary and unnecessary for humaneness is study, and implementing the necessary ones at all levels is evidence and accomplishment (MVD, p. 161). The journey to realisation begins with methodical study, whose field is definitive understanding (avdharana) (AVD, p. 223). Dedication carries study to realisation: study for the human goal in the light of justice, dharma, and truth occurs through dedication, and dedication leads to realisation (MVD, p. 150).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Study proceeds by two means that correct each other, inquiry while studying and study while inquiring (AVD, p. 225). Instruction by sermon always carries a possibility of delusion, and a tradition’s commands remain sermons or information until they become studiable, that is, until their intent is understood in logic and behaviour (AVD, p. 225). Each person examines any presentation with their own imagination and freedom of action and accepts or rejects it on that basis (AVD, p. 226). The darshan’s formula for the relation between accepting and knowing is short: believe what is known; know what is believed (MVD, p. 12).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The older vocabulary of practice is kept and redefined around study. Sadhana is effort towards self-improvement, whose point of fulfilment is awakening (AVD, pp. 233–234); practice (abhyas) is carrying the awakening and prosperity so attained into behaviour and teaching as comprehensive resolution (AVD, p. 234); and the triad of aim, seeker, and means is reconstituted, with every human the seeker of awakening, awakening the aim, and the method of study the means (AVD, p. 224; MVD, p. 322). Experimentation is the endeavour, continued until it succeeds, to meet a human need by instilling usefulness and aesthetic value in natural abundance (MVD, p. 56). Humans have undertaken studies, experiments, explorations, and practices for realisation, reflected in humaneness and higher humaneness (MVD, p. 302), and the study and practice of the mediative activity, atma, as presented in this darshan, leads to integrality — justice, dharma, and truth-based behaviour, thought, and realisation together (MVD, p. 303).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.7 Upasana redefined

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The inherited sense of upasana is devotional practice towards deities, or ritual (MVD, p. 4; JV, p. 9). In this darshan its content is different altogether:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Upasana is an important part of human jeevan. It is the process of refining and transforming the fundamental tendencies, and this study also transforms sanskar and essential nature.” — KD, p. 30

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The fundamental tendencies are the antahkarana’s hope, thought, desire, and resoluteness (KD, p. 36), and upasana is itself a form of study: until one is complete in one’s own dharma, upasana continues in the form of study (KD, p. 38), and the attainments of the best upasana are the completeness of study (KD, p. 37). Its root sense is attaining togetherness through proper means, which requires diligence and practice (KD, p. 30). It is of three kinds: kutastha upasana, undertaken for complete realisation; rupastha upasana, undertaken to approach a form endowed with magnificence; and atmastha upasana, which is reflection itself and to which every human being is bound (KD, p. 31). The deities of the traditions are reinterpreted within the same scheme as bodiless jeevans — elemental, deific, and divine selves — ranked by awakening (KD, p. 31), and the upasana directed to each yields base learning, sub-learning, or learning accordingly (KD, p. 32).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Upasana is education and orderliness in its own nature (KD, p. 42); its chief utility lies in immersion in universal values (KD, p. 35); at the root of all upasanas the aim is undivided society and universal orderliness (KD, p. 35); and upasanas exist only for the capacity for awakening, not for decline (KD, p. 36). Its success condition is stated: upasana must contain the aim, the seeker, and the means together, and their integrality brings success while their separation brings failure (KD, p. 38). Its disciplines include the classical restraints: truthfulness, non-violence, non-possession, and non-stealing are practised as restraint (KD, p. 39); gratitude is the beginning-to-end basis of restraint; and a mantra is any meaningful word whose meaning and nature are attained by consistently remembering that meaning (KD, p. 40). Upasana that takes a symbol for its goal is judged secondary and unsocial to the extent of its incompleteness, because in it the human goal is neither clarified nor attained (KD, p. 42).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The consequence is that practice in this darshan has no private phase. Wisdom and jeevan-value — resolution and prosperity — are the direct results of upasana, and sociality is naturally contained in them; the dignity of human jeevan is the impetus to behave with one’s equal and to practise towards greater awakening, and this is real upasana (KD, p. 37). The samadhi route is the reverse case, in which the seeker cannot take part in family or society while practising (§1.3). Family Relationships and Values §1.4.2 draws the family-scale consequence: the practice begins in the relationships one is born into.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.8 Yog, dhyan, and the vocabulary of discipline

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Yog in this darshan is union, of two kinds, unification and togetherness (MVD, p. 42). It names how units come together rather than a technique of posture or breath, but it is not only a term of physical ontology. Mediative behaviour, thought, and realisation constitute pre-existing yog, continuously available and ever present, while the development and decline of a unit depend on the unions it enters, development-oriented or decline-oriented (MVD, p. 159). Realisation happens only of pre-existing yog — the omnipresent reality from which no entity is ever separate — while proximity and accumulation belong only to attainable yog (MVD, p. 302). Yog is therefore necessary for realisation (MVD, p. 302); every human is awakened only through yog (MVD, p. 304); and the realisation of the self is attained through yog in the tradition, meaning the union of body and jeevan and union with awakened humans for awakening (MVD, p. 301). This is why humans seek association with those more awakened than themselves (MVD, p. 274). A reader carrying the modern sense of “yoga” into these passages will find no postures and no breath-control. What they will find is an account of the company and orientation through which awakening happens.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Dhyan is redefined in the same spirit. The meditation the traditions recommend aims to limit thought to one point until thought ceases (AVD, pp. 164, 219). The darshan gives concentration a different object:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Concentration involves focusing mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi for understanding, and focusing them for the purpose of evidence after understanding and realisation.” — MVD, p. 284

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The object of concentration is the comprehension of meaning and its evidence, and all humans possess the capacity for concentration (MVD, pp. 284–285). Concentration in this sense belongs to the inward regulation (antarniyaman) through which atma-bodh happens, and atma-bodh is the highest accomplishment of concentration (MVD, p. 286).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The ascetic vocabulary is reworked the same way. Dispassion is inclination towards the ideal without inclination elsewhere, and a chain of identities joins it to non-attachment, non-doership, non-accumulation, fearlessness and prosperity, heavenliness, humility, supreme detachment (par-vairagya), yog, realisation in omnipresence, mediation, authenticity, and liberation from delusion (MVD, p. 157). Supreme detachment is liberation from the flaws of excess, deficiency, and omission that stand against awakening (MVD, pp. 157–158). Non-accumulation means resolution and prosperity rather than poverty, and heaven becomes the heavenliness of just living (MVD, p. 160). Initiation (diksha) is accepting a definite method of behaviour and conduct as an unbroken pledge (MVD, p. 309). The ideal (ishta) of devotional practice becomes self-driven reverence, trust, and dedication towards coexistence together with complete knowledge (MVD, p. 80). And samyama has, besides the founder’s method of §1.4, the ordinary sense of restraint: being regulated in humane thought, behaviour, and vocation (MVD, p. 337).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Devotion belongs to this vocabulary too. Bhakti is the activity of becoming liberated from fear and delusion, the expression, communication, and exposition of prayer joined with seva, and an expression of total dedication (MVD, p. 339), where dedication is the continuous endeavour of attaining and evidencing complete awakening (MVD, p. 340). The expression, communication, and exposition of values with evidence, maintained in human tradition upon awakening, is love and devotion (MVD, p. 307). Devotedness (anurag) and love (prem) towards the ideal in the form of coexistence are among the mandatory conditions of realisation (MVD, p. 317; §1.12). The darshan’s practice vocabulary is therefore wider than study, experiment, and practice: it keeps upasana, sadhana, abhyas, dhyan, yog, samyama, bhakti, diksha, and vairagya, and gives each a content defined by understanding and conduct. What it rejects is set out in §1.15.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.9 The ten activities of jeevan and the 122 conducts

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan is a constitutionally complete atom whose nucleus is atma and whose four orbits are buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun (MVD, p. 78; AVD, p. 87). These five are its inexhaustible strengths (bal), and hope, thought, desire, resoluteness (ritambhara), and authenticity (pramanikta) are its inexhaustible powers (shakti) (MVD, pp. 75, 84; AVD, p. 151). Each faculty has two activities, one of reflection and one of projection: realisation and authenticity in atma, enlightenment and resolve in buddhi, contemplation and visualisation in chitta, deliberation and analysis in vritti, and taste and selection in mun (JV, pp. 73, 92–93). Every jeevan continuously operates through these ten activities, whether in delusion or in awakening (JV, p. 73).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In delusion only four and a half of them are effective. Selection and taste in mun, analysis in vritti, visualisation in chitta, and half of deliberation — deliberation confined to what is pleasant, healthy, and profitable — are sufficient for the five senses and the four instincts, and what they produce does not become the content of contemplation (JV, pp. 73–74; AVD, p. 152; MVD, p. 79). They come into play in that order from infancy (JV, p. 94). Awakening the remaining five and a half, which happens through understanding, is what a humane mentality requires, and awakening is the evidence of all ten in behaviour (JV, p. 74). Upon awakening, jeevan evidences all ten through the realisation-based way (MVD, p. 79).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The ten are the generic activities. In awakening their detailed content becomes evident as 122 activities:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi and atma are integral in jeevan. In awakened jeevan, its faculties or activities that become evident in the tradition in the form of strength & power or state & motion are as follows: atma has two faculties, buddhi has four, chitta has sixteen, vritti has thirty-six, and mun has sixty-four. Therefore, 122 activities are found in human jeevan in the form of strength & power, that is, in state & motion. Each person can demonstrate all of the above activities.” — MVD, p. 323

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The 122 are tabulated as the conducts of awakened jeevan, sixty-one pairs of a reflective and a projective activity, and each is defined (AVD, pp. 91–94; MVD, pp. 328–348). They include most of what the contemplative and devotional traditions treat as spiritual attainments. In atma the pair is realisation in existence and the authenticity of ultimate bliss. In buddhi the pairs are bliss and definiteness, and existence and fearlessness. In chitta they include revelation and memory, contentment and abundance, love and non-otherness, and reverence (shraddha) and devoutness (pujyata). In vritti they include learning and intelligence, peace and kindness, grace and compassion, uprightness and forgiveness, gratitude and humility, truth and dharma, justice and sensitivity, absolute-oneness and intrepidity, and restraint and law. In mun they include devotion and immersion, care and generosity, respect and cordiality, and affection and dedication (AVD, pp. 91–94; MVD, pp. 323–340). Bliss, love, reverence, devotion, forgiveness, gratitude, restraint, and absolute-oneness are thus not states to be attained in withdrawal. They are named conducts of awakened jeevan, and many of them are directed to other people.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This is the point at which the account of practice becomes specific. Practice is not aimed at producing a state; it is aimed at making effective activities that jeevan already has. Knowledge of jeevan is its constitution together with the inspection, examination, and survey of its activities (AVD, pp. 86–87), which makes one’s own activities a field of study. The systematic study of the awakened conducts is the subject of a separate treatise, Manav Sanchetnavadi Manovigyan (AVD, p. 151).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.10 How the activities are activated and refined

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The defect practice addresses is located with unusual precision. Under delusion, hope in mun is based on sensation, thought in vritti follows that hope, desire in chitta follows that thought, and buddhi, turned away from atma, supports deluded visualisation and desire (MVD, pp. 204, 275). In awakening the direction reverses: hope in mun accords with vritti, thought in vritti with chitta, desire in chitta with the enlightenment of buddhi, and the enlightenment of buddhi with atma’s realisation in existence; the resulting reflection and projection form the awakened jeevan cycle (MVD, p. 275). Practice is therefore the repair of a circuit rather than the accumulation of states (The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Awakening begins with the strength of contemplation, whereas the bondage of delusion runs on the powers of hope, thought, and desire (AVD, p. 151). Study supplies contemplation with its content. As definitive understanding grows, the perspectives of justice, dharma, and truth become active in the deliberation of vritti; their direct recognition follows in chitta, enlightenment and acceptance in buddhi, and their realisation in atma, confirmed in contemplation (AVD, pp. 86, 223–224; MVD, p. 126). Each faculty reaches its complete development by receiving the signal of the one within it. Mun does so by acquiring the receptivity for just behaviour on accepting the signals of vritti; vritti by accepting the signals of chitta, that is, by the ability to form dharma-based thought; chitta by the capacity for creative visualisation according to the signals of buddhi in the presence of truth; buddhi by accepting the signals of atma; and atma in realisation in coexistence (MVD, pp. 322–323). Each step has its mark. When mun receives the signal of vritti, just behaviour and affection follow; when vritti receives that of chitta, peace; when chitta receives that of buddhi, contentment and self-governed living; and when buddhi receives that of atma, enlightenment of the self, atma-bodh, and resolve in truth (MVD, pp. 282–283). Concurrence of mun and vritti is happiness, of vritti and chitta peace, of chitta and buddhi contentment, and of buddhi and atma bliss; the eternal concurrence of atma with the omnipresent is ultimate bliss (MVD, p. 327).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The conditions of each step are named as well. The reflection of hope succeeds in the absence of crime, of thought in the absence of injustice, of desire in the absence of attachment, and of resolve in the absence of ignorance. Each requires its support: the influence of orderliness for behaviour without crime, of social conduct for thought without injustice, of study and sanskar for desire without attachment, and inward regulation or concentration for a buddhi without ignorance. Only then does reflection succeed; otherwise it fails (MVD, p. 284). The channelling of jeevan’s energies towards awakening runs through curiosity in mun, enthusiasm in vritti, delight in chitta, elation and immersion in buddhi, and realisation in atma, and it requires the inward regulation of those energies (MVD, p. 77).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Refinement is the work of upasana (§1.7), and its object is definite: the fundamental tendencies of hope, thought, desire, and resoluteness, which are refined when they are no longer wasted. The awakening of activity-power is the right use, rather than the waste, of the powers exercised through the senses; the awakening of desire-power is the right use of the fundamental tendencies; and the awakening of knowledge-power is right enlightenment together with complete realisation. This awakening of the three powers is the supreme attainment of human jeevan and the purpose of upasana (KD, p. 36). What refinement removes is delusion’s excess, deficiency, and omission in visualisation and its over-, under-, and mis-evaluation (MVD, p. 286; AVD, p. 55), and the level of awakening a person has reached is judged by their attachment or non-attachment to the body’s instincts and the objects of the senses (MVD, p. 203).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Once awakened, realisation flows outward through the same faculties. Its enlightenment is in buddhi; its awareness (prateeti) arises where buddhi meets chitta; its comprehension (abhas) where chitta meets vritti; and its perception (bhas) where vritti meets mun, showing as the taste of values and the selection of relationships (MVD, p. 99). Just behaviour is the perception of truth, resolved thought its comprehension, and contemplation its awareness (MVD, p. 316). This outward course is how the 122 conducts become evident in relationships (§1.9), and it is why awakening is evidenced through the combined activity of all five faculties (MVD, p. 203).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.11 The ladder: sakshatkar, bodh, anubhav, praman

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realisation is not a single act. It is the third rung of a four-stage sequence — sakshatkar, bodh, anubhav, praman — whose members are linked so tightly that each is said to be the next: realisation is the ultimate evidence, evidence is understanding, understanding is manifest, the manifest is resolution and work and behaviour, work and behaviour is evidence, evidence is awakened tradition, and awakened tradition is coexistence (MVD, p. 12). The stages fall on the faculties of §1.9: affirmation of truth in the form of coexistence through study is manan in mun, tulan in vritti by the qualitative method, sakshatkar in chitta, and bodh in buddhi (MVD, p. 126). Realisation-based bodh issues in resolve, sakshatkar, realisation-based contemplation and thought, and finally evidence (MVD, p. 99). Nagraj describes the same order in the first person: realisation attained after revelation (sakshatkar) and definitive understanding (avdharna bodh), contemplation following from that enlightenment (JV, p. 62).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The relation between the stages is defined through definitive understanding:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Knowing, believing & recognising itself is definitive understanding. Attaining the point of satisfaction in these itself is realisation. Expressing it in actions & behaviour, and in systems, is authenticity.” — AVD, p. 224

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realisation on this definition adds no new object to what definitive understanding already holds. It is the point at which that understanding reaches satisfaction, and authenticity is its expression in conduct and in orderliness. In a recorded session Nagraj puts the same point directly. Asked what further is understood in anubhav beyond bodh, he answers that nothing is: what occurs in sakshatkar becomes firm (22:28). He adds that if sakshatkar succeeds the remaining three stages follow of themselves, as acceptance or rejection follows ordinary seeing (03:03–03:30), and that praman is the power to bring about bodh in another (04:43). The weight of the sequence therefore falls on sakshatkar, which he calls the success of study (12:54).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The fourth stage is not a report issued after the fact. Evidence is awakened tradition (MVD, p. 12), and only awakened humans are recognisable in the seer status (MVD, p. 33). In the same session anubhav is given the second name drashtapad, the seat of the seer, and praman the name jagriti, awakening (13:09, 17:30, 21:13).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Establishment in the seer status is also the printed definition of tadavalokan, continuous observance of the ideal, and that definition belongs to the darshan’s reinterpretation of devotional union. In the knowledge order, pursuit of the ideal (ishta-sevan) aims at oneness with it, accordance with it, abiding near it, and continuous observance of it; the ideal is self-driven reverence, trust, and dedication towards coexistence together with complete knowledge; and the way to that accordance is realisation itself (MVD, p. 80):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Realisation in coexistence itself is the way of absolute-accordance and absolute-resonance (tadakar), because law, regulation, balance, justice, dharma, and truth become evident as a result of realisation.” — MVD, p. 80

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The prefix tat- in these terms indicates awakening (MVD, p. 80), and awakening is the human ideal (MVD, pp. 306–307). The vocabulary of becoming one with a chosen deity is kept, its object becomes awakening in coexistence, and the means of accordance becomes study: through study one comes into absolute-resonance and absolute-accordance with understanding (MVD, p. 150), just as the inner faculties, brought into absolute-resonance with an aim, become intense in that aim (KD, p. 40).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.12 Two paths, preconditions, and the teacher

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: For a person who is not the discoverer there are two alternatives:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Such a process is of two kinds: One - Exploration. Two - Following, Emulation, Study.” — MVD, p. 280

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Exploration is an inventive realisation which the seeker studies comprehensively, from the extreme of decline to the highest development and awakening. It is the route of a seeker accomplished in samadhi, who establishes themself in just behaviour and dharma-based thought through practice and then develops the capacity for deific and divine humaneness and for realisation of the omnipresent (MVD, pp. 280–281). The second path has two programmes: following or emulating just behaviour, and being and abiding in resolved, dharma-based thought. Firmness and dedication in these two give the authority for realisation of truth (MVD, p. 282).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The darshan also settles which path is for whom. It asks why its author, having reached awakening by the traditional methods, does not recommend them, and replies that its own method is practicable. The silence method yields only self-limited happiness, no one can be assured of success within a lifetime, and silence is against the natural manifestation of jeevan (AVD, pp. 72–74). The two ways it offers are exploration, and inquiry together with study (AVD, p. 225). In the recorded session Nagraj adds that for everyone to undertake samadhi–samyama and exploration is impractical, and that study is the method by which everyone can arrive (34:07).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The conditions of realisation are demanding. Realisation in knowledge requires the capacity, ability, and receptivity for delusion-free knowledge, non-otherness, devotedness, and love towards the ideal in the form of coexistence, and these are achieved through just behaviour, resolved thought, and full dedication in obedience to a realised human being (MVD, p. 317). Delusion-free knowledge is knowing, understanding, and imparting the understanding of realities as they are; non-otherness is its continuity; devotedness is the continuity of non-otherness, an earnest endeavour for freedom from delusion; and love is the continuity of non-otherness together with devotedness, the combined expression of kindness, grace, and compassion (MVD, p. 317). Dharma, unlike form, property, and essential nature, can be realised only through study and adherence to the step-by-step instructions of one who has attained realisation (MVD, p. 273).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The teacher’s role is correspondingly large. The authentic human is the teacher in whose proximity study takes place (MVD, p. 150); in study imparted by the guru through the realisation-based way, justice, dharma, and truth are accepted in the student’s buddhi upon direct recognition (MVD, p. 99); awakened humans are the natural guides of the unawakened, and humans aspire to awaken through their own inspiration and through the inspiration, grace, and compassion of those more awakened (MVD, p. 287); and the teacher is the bearer and carrier of the evidence of awakening, with the literature as its guideline (AVD, p. 261). Alongside these statements stand the principles of §1.6: each person examines any presentation and accepts or rejects it (AVD, p. 226), and commands remain information until they become studiable (AVD, p. 225). The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.6 records the transmission requirements in outline, and §6.4 examines how the two sides of the teacher’s role fit together.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.13 How realisation is evidenced

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Because the darshan refuses to let an inner state serve as its own credential (§1.3), it needs public marks, and it names three kinds of evidence: realisation, behaviour, and experiment (MVD, p. 12). The awakened human, not scripture or instrument, is the basis of evidence (SB, p. 5). Understanding must be conveyable: “The proof of our comprehension lies in our ability to convey it to others” (JV, p. 26), and making just behaviour, resolved thought, and realisation in truth understandable, knowable, and practicable through language is the work of realised humans (MVD, p. 316). Conduct must change: integrality is justice, dharma, and truth-based behaviour, thought, and realisation together (MVD, p. 303); the absence of mistakes and crimes in behaviour characterises complete awakening (MVD, p. 285); and the ability to provide justice is the evidence of liberation from bondage (AVD, pp. 172–173). Work with nature must succeed, since experimentation is the endeavour continued until natural abundance is made useful (MVD, p. 56). And the change must be reproducible in tradition: an awakened human evidences awakening by paving the path for the deluded (MVD, p. 273), and awakening completeness is evidenced in participation in the whole of orderliness together with expression, communication, and exposition (AVD, pp. 259–260).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The darshan grades what these marks show. Humans are perceived as animalistic, demonic, humane, deific, and divine according to their awakening (MVD, p. 314). Those who have realised the truth and live by justice and dharma are awakened, those whose thought and behaviour accord with justice and dharma are half-developed, and those who accord with justice alone are partially developed (MVD, p. 160). The darshan also states the criterion that is meant to make these marks evidence of truth rather than of competence alone: truth is what is uniformly realised everywhere (MVD, p. 35), and the authenticity of realisation is the same in, by, and for all human beings (AVD, p. 61).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: On the darshan’s own architecture these marks are not tests applied from outside to an inner event. Praman is the fourth stage of realisation itself (§1.11). §6.3 considers what follows for their evidential force.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.14 The circle the darshan states itself

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The dependencies of realisation are set out without concealing that they close:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The ability of realisation in knowledge depends on human awakening; human awakening depends on sanskars; development of sanskars depends on environment, study & endeavour; environment, study & endeavour depend on humaneness and higher humaneness; humaneness and higher humaneness depend on the ability of realisation in knowledge.” — MVD, p. 290

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These dependencies connect realisation, formation, study, and conduct. Learning can begin through study and participation before complete awakening: the outward expressed values can be learnt before their counterparts are established in state (Axiology Value Theory §§1.4, 1.8), and belief can follow knowing and knowing can follow belief (MVD, p. 12). The question of how a learner evaluates the teaching and progresses towards establishment is examined separately in §6.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.15 What the darshan rejects

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The account is defined as much by exclusion as by prescription, but what it excludes are paths and their assumptions, not the vocabulary of practice. Mystery-based idealistic contemplation failed to accomplish the study of the human being, as did materialism-centred ideology (MVD, p. 3). In place of devotion–renunciation, isolation, accumulation, comfort-seeking, and hedonism, the darshan presents coexistence and, within orderliness, resolution, prosperity, and fearlessness (SB, p. 5). Renunciation, non-accumulation, detachment, and devotion, pursued as ideals, have drawn immense courage and dedication and produced no undivided society (JV, p. 105), and the character of renunciation and of devotion-ism is itself individualistic (SB, p. 238). Idealism takes ideal persons as its evidence, with devotion and renunciation as the criterion for recognising them (AVD, p. 62). Faith, defined as accepting the existence of something without knowing it (AVD, p. 17), rests at its root on the expectation that wishes shaped by fear and temptation will be fulfilled (SB, p. 238), and adoration pleads with an omnipotent unknown to turn inability into ability and remains individual-centred (AVD, p. 233). Seeking refuge in God as the real father and mother yields no human (JV, p. 57). Instruction by sermon risks delusion (AVD, p. 225), upasana that takes the symbol for the goal is secondary and unsocial (KD, p. 42), and the absorbed state itself yields no knowing (§1.3).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: What survives these exclusions is not a bare minimum. Devotion, reverence, dispassion, restraint, concentration, and union are kept and redefined by understanding and conduct (§1.8), and most of them reappear among the conducts of awakened jeevan (§1.9). The path that remains is study of a stated system, the refinement of tendency, the activation of all ten activities, and evidence in relationship and conduct. It removes the traditional shortcuts, including the one the founder was told was the only way.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.16 Method, evidence, and what Madhyasth Darshan establishes

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Separating the kinds of claim matters here more than in most of these studies, because the founder’s report does evidential work throughout.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Some claims are first-person historical report: that samadhi was attained and contained no knowing event; that samyama was redesigned, directed at space, and produced realisation of coexistence (MVD, pp. 4, 7; JV, pp. 12–14; AVD, p. 72). These are testimony about how the system arose — strong evidence of what one careful practitioner found, and no evidence that others would find the same.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Some are definitional within the system: spirituality as understanding of the omnipresent (AVD, p. 236); realisation as realisation in coexistence and as the satisfaction of definitive understanding (MVD, p. 316; AVD, p. 224); mystery as incapacity to attain or convey understanding (MVD, p. 273); upasana as refinement of the fundamental tendencies (KD, p. 30); concentration as focusing the faculties for understanding and evidence (MVD, p. 284); bhakti as liberation from fear and delusion expressed in dedication (MVD, p. 339); yog as union (MVD, p. 42).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Some are structural claims about jeevan: ten activities, four and a half effective in delusion, and 122 conducts in awakening (JV, p. 73; MVD, pp. 79, 323). They depend on the darshan’s account of the jeevan atom, examined in The Ontology of Coexistence and The Epistemology of Coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Some are methodological prescriptions that could be followed and reported on: the two paths and their programmes (MVD, pp. 280–282), the conditions and supports of reflection (MVD, p. 284), study together with inquiry (AVD, p. 225), and experimentation continued to success (MVD, p. 56).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: And one is a negative epistemic claim of general force: that a contentless absorbed state cannot serve as evidence. This is the darshan’s most transferable contribution, and it does not depend on accepting anything else in the system.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A further class enters with §§1.11 and 1.12: recorded oral teaching from a 2010 session at Amarkantak. It corroborates printed doctrine at several points — that realisation adds nothing to what sakshatkar recognises, and that exploration is not the general route — and it states some things not located in the printed texts reviewed here, such as the names drashtapad and jagriti for the third and fourth stages and the automatic succession of stages after sakshatkar. The Editorial Notes set out how this material is used.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta holds that liberation is not produced by practice at all, because it is not a state to be attained. What practice does is remove the ignorance that obscures what is already the case. Every feature of its path follows from that, and it makes Advaita the sharpest possible contrast to a darshan whose founder went looking for an event and reported not finding one.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.1 Moksha as eternally accomplished

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Shankara’s Brahma Sutra Bhashya treats liberation as eternally accomplished, obscured by avidya, and disclosed by knowledge (BSB 1.1.4). The self is not altered by realisation; the superimposition of self and not-self is removed, which is the subject of the Adhyasa Bhashya prefacing the commentary. Because the goal is not produced, practice cannot be its efficient cause — a point Advaita presses against ritualist and yogic accounts alike (BSB 1.1.4, 2.1.3).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: This is where the traditions are closest. Both hold that the reality to be realised is already present: for Advaita the self was never other than Brahman, and for Madhyasth Darshan no unit is ever separate from the omnipresent reality whose realisation is the human goal (MVD, pp. 302–303, 317). Both deny that an achieved state is the goal. They differ over what the reality is, what the knower is, and what the world is. Advaita identifies the self with Brahman and treats the world as mithya. Madhyasth Darshan holds that atma — the seer, the self, the seat of knowledge — is the nucleus of a finite jeevan unit saturated in the omnipresent (MVD, p. 210), that Brahma is truth and the world is perpetual (MVD, p. 13), and that realisation requires a capacity that must be developed and evidenced (MVD, p. 302).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.2 Qualification before instruction

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita is exacting about what a seeker must bring. The sadhana-chatushtaya comprises discrimination between eternal and non-eternal (viveka), dispassion (vairagya), the six treasures beginning with tranquillity and self-restraint, and the intense desire for liberation (mumukshutva); the Vivekachudamani sets out these qualifications and the supporting virtues (vv. 17–20, 69, 82). The Gita’s list of divine qualities serves the same preparatory function (16.1–16.3).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The role is precise: these qualify a person to receive teaching and do not themselves constitute knowledge. Advaita therefore has a two-stage structure — become fit, then be taught — with an explicit account of what fitness consists in. Madhyasth Darshan also states preconditions — the capacity for delusion-free knowledge, non-otherness, devotedness, and love towards the ideal, achieved through just behaviour, resolved thought, and dedicated obedience to a realised human (MVD, p. 317) — but it places them before realisation rather than before instruction, and it holds that the capacity for realisation is the right of every human being (MVD, pp. 285, 302).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.3 Hearing, reflection, and sustained contemplation

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The path proper is shravana, manana, and nididhyasana — hearing the teaching from a qualified teacher, reasoning it through until doubt is removed, and sustained contemplation until it is no longer merely understood but immediate. The Brihadaranyaka’s instruction to Maitreyi is the classical locus (BU 2.4.5). Sruti is the means of knowledge for what perception and inference cannot reach, with reasoning subordinate and confirmatory.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The negative discipline is neti neti — not this, not this (BU 2.3.6) — and the identification is tat tvam asi (CU 6.8.7). What removes ignorance is a knowledge event mediated by language, which is why Advaita can be uncompromising about scripture while remaining unimpressed by absorption.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.4 The disputed status of samadhi

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita’s own position on absorbed states is more divided than popular accounts suggest, and the division matters for the comparison. Shankara subordinates yoga to knowledge: samadhi may steady the mind but does not by itself remove ignorance, since what removes ignorance is knowledge and nothing else (BSB 2.1.3). Later texts within the tradition are warmer — the Vivekachudamani praises absorption and treats it as near-indispensable, and its authorship is disputed for this among other reasons. The Mandukya material on the fourth state, turiya, describes a condition beyond waking, dream, and deep sleep (MU, vv. 3–7), which is not the same as recommending a technique for reaching it.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Nagraj’s finding in §1.3 bears on Advaita practice as he encountered it. His doubts began with the Vedanta literature on bondage and liberation, his practice followed the instructions for nididhyasan as well as for samadhi, and he counts the resulting thoughtless state under both names (AVD, p. 72). On Shankara’s account nididhyasana is sustained contemplation of the meaning of the teaching, not thoughtlessness, and that samadhi contains no knowing event is what one should expect. The finding therefore does not straightforwardly refute Advaita, and the disagreement turns partly on what nididhyasana is. Where the traditions genuinely part is on what does the work of knowing: for Advaita, sruti-mediated knowledge culminating in immediacy; for the darshan, study culminating in definitive understanding, its satisfaction in realisation, and its evidence in conduct.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.5 After realisation

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The jivanmukta continues to act, and the Gita supplies the account: prescribed action (3.8) performed without attachment (3.9, 3.19), and action for the holding-together of the world (3.20, 3.25–26). Conduct expresses realisation without being its cause or its evidence in the darshan’s sense. Advaita does not require the liberated person to establish an order, transmit a system, or produce social outcomes, and it does not treat failure to do so as counting against realisation.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan uses the same name, jeevan-mukta, for one freed from delusion while living, and gives it the opposite emphasis. The jeevan-mukta is free of suffering over past and future, and nurturing and advancing society is their essential nature (MVD, pp. 81, 157); the one who is evidence in kaivalya has no need of further bodily journeys and remains an inspiration after the body dies (AVD, p. 261).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.6 Method, evidence, and what Advaita establishes

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita’s method is scriptural testimony for the supersensible, disciplined reasoning against it, and contemplation to make it immediate, with qualification as a precondition. Its enduring achievements here are two: the argument that nothing produced can be the final good, hence no state is liberation; and a rigorous account of how a knowledge event, rather than an experience, could remove ignorance. What it does not offer, by its own lights, is public evidence of realisation. The criterion is the knower’s own conviction: when someone knows in his heart that he has realised Brahman while still holding the body, no one else can deny it (BSB 4.1.15). The Gita’s characteristics of the one steady in wisdom describe such a knower (BG 2.55–72), but Shankara presents them as disciplines for the seeker rather than as tests of another’s knowledge (BG 2.55, commentary). The tradition accepts this internal criterion rather than treating it as a gap.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: The subject is not outside modern philosophy’s range; it has been worked on from several directions, and the results are unusually relevant to the claims in §1.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.1 Philosophy as spiritual exercise

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Hadot’s Philosophy as a Way of Life argued that ancient philosophy was not primarily a body of doctrine but a set of spiritual exercises — attention, meditation on death, examination of conscience, memorisation of precepts — whose aim was the transformation of the practitioner. Doctrine served practice rather than the reverse. Foucault’s late lectures on the care of the self and askesis develop the same material toward techniques of self-formation.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: This displaces the assumption that “spiritual practice” names something religious and other than philosophy. It also supplies the closest Western structural analogue to the darshan’s position: study whose point is transformation, doctrine that is not idle, exercises that are not withdrawal from the world. Hadot’s ancients, like this darshan, treat the philosophical life as continuous with conduct in the city rather than as preparation for leaving it.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.2 Religious and mystical experience: perennialism against constructivism

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: James’s Varieties of Religious Experience established the field by treating such experiences as data with describable marks — ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity — and by taking their fruits as the test of their worth. Stace’s Mysticism and Philosophy argued for a common core across traditions, distinguishing extrovertive from introvertive mysticism and treating the latter as a contentless unity underlying diverse interpretations. Katz’s “Language, Epistemology, and Mysticism” reversed this: there are no unmediated experiences, and a tradition’s concepts shape the experience itself, not merely its report. Forman and others replied by defending a pure consciousness event stripped of content (SEP Mysticism).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: The dispute bears directly on the darshan’s negative finding. Nagraj reports a state in which hope, thought, and desire were silent, the awareness of “I am” remained, nothing further occurred, and nothing could be described (MVD, p. 7; JV, pp. 12–13). That is close to what perennialists describe as a pure consciousness event, and it is precisely what a constructivist would predict a Vedically and tantrically trained practitioner to reach and to find unhelpful. That the same report can be read as evidence for either position shows how little a phenomenological description settles.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.3 The epistemology of religious experience

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Alston’s Perceiving God is the most developed defence of the idea that experience of God can be a source of justified belief, arguing that “mystical perceptual practice” is not shown unreliable merely because it lacks the cross-checking available to sense perception, and that demanding such checks begs the question. The standard objections are the absence of independent verification, the diversity of incompatible reports across traditions, and the difficulty of specifying reliability conditions (SEP Religious Experience).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan sits at an odd angle to this literature. It agrees with the critics that a contemplative state without describable content cannot be evidence — indeed it says so more sharply than the critics do. But it then claims realisation with statable content and offers conveyability, conduct, and experiment as the cross-checks Alston is accused of lacking. Whether those checks are the right kind is §4.4’s question.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.4 Transformative experience

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Paul’s Transformative Experience formalises a problem the contemplative traditions have always faced without naming it. Some experiences are epistemically transformative: one cannot know what they are like, or what one will value afterwards, without having had them. Decisions about whether to undergo them therefore cannot be made by ordinary expected-value reasoning from present values, because the relevant values are among the things that change.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: This is precisely the structure of a call to practice. The darshan’s demand that understanding be conveyable before it is accepted is an attempt to escape it — to make the case in terms available to the unawakened. Paul’s analysis suggests why that is hard: if realisation changes what one counts as evidence and what one values, the pre-realisation assessment cannot be authoritative and the post-realisation assessment cannot be neutral. Advaita’s qualification requirement (§2.2) is the same problem handled by admission criteria rather than by argument.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.5 Contemplative science and its reckoning

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Empirical work on meditation has established real effects and has also undergone a methodological correction that matters more than the effects. Neuroimaging has found trait and state differences in long-term practitioners (Lutz et al. 2004), and clinical trials support moderate benefits for some conditions. But Van Dam and colleagues’ “Mind the Hype” documented systematic problems across the field — inconsistent definitions of mindfulness, weak or absent active controls, small samples, and publication bias — and Lindahl and colleagues’ study of the varieties of contemplative experience catalogued a wide range of adverse and destabilising effects in Western Buddhist practitioners, effects that traditional literatures acknowledge and modern secular programmes had largely omitted. Thompson has argued that findings of this kind cannot carry the epistemic conclusions sometimes drawn from them (Thompson 2020).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Two conclusions bear on this study. Contemplative practice demonstrably changes people, so a tradition claiming transformation is not making an empty claim. And nothing in this literature reaches the epistemic question: measuring that a practice alters attention, affect, or self-report says nothing about whether the resulting understanding is true. The science can corroborate the darshan’s claim that practice transforms and is structurally unable to corroborate its claim that the transformation is a knowing.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.6 Method, evidence, and what modern work establishes

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Modern philosophy establishes that transformation-oriented practice belongs to philosophy’s own history rather than outside it; that no description of a contemplative state settles whether its content is given or constructed; that the demand for cross-checking is reasonable but not obviously decisive against experiential justification; and that appraising transformative experience from outside is structurally difficult. Contemplative science establishes that practice has measurable effects, that the field’s early claims outran its methods, and that adverse effects are real. None of it establishes what realisation is or whether anyone has attained it.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4. Comparison

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.1 Criteria for comparison

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: The three positions are compared on eight questions: what the goal is; whether it is already present; what practice produces; what the decisive means is; the status of absorbed states; what counts as evidence of attainment; the place of conduct and relationship; and what liberation and the world afterwards are.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.2 Cross-tradition summary

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Modern philosophy and science The goal Realisation of existence as coexistence — of all units saturated in the omnipresent; liberation from delusion Moksha — recognition of what is eternally the case No settled goal;
